analysis.one_liner: Caps the size of the biggest banks and forces them to hold more capital against losses.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2010 with 7 cosponsors and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up; it died without a vote or hearing.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have capped how big any single bank holding company could get: no more than 10% of the nation's insured deposits, nondeposit borrowing capped at 2% of the U.S. economy (3% for nonbank financial companies), and a requirement that big banks hold at least 6 cents of their own capital for every dollar of assets. It would also have forced over-leveraged firms to shrink, and required companies to put all their assets and liabilities, including off-balance-sheet deals, on their public balance sheets. The aim was to make the largest banks small enough or well-capitalized enough that their failure would not drag down the economy or trigger taxpayer bailouts.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers, who were exposed to the cost of rescuing 'too big to fail' banks after the 2008 crisis; smaller and regional banks, which would compete on a more even field; and investors, who would see a fuller picture of company debts on balance sheets.

how_it_helps.text: Caps any bank holding company at 10% of all insured U.S. deposits and orders the Federal Reserve to force violators to sell assets to come into compliance [S2][S3].

Requires bank holding companies and financial companies to hold tier 1 capital of at least 6% of average total assets, with a matching balance-sheet leverage ratio, and directs regulators to impose corrective action on violators [S2][S3].
Limits nondeposit liabilities to 2% of U.S. GDP for bank holding companies and 3% for nonbank financial companies, counting off-balance-sheet liabilities [S2][S3].

Directs the SEC to require public companies to record all assets and liabilities, including off-balance-sheet financings, on their balance sheets, with disclosure rules for liabilities they cannot quantify [S2][S3].
Requires the Federal Reserve to run an annual capital assessment estimating losses, revenues, and reserve needs for large financial firms and report to Congress [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The largest bank holding companies and big nonbank financial companies, which would have had to raise capital, sell assets, or break apart to comply within one to three years of enactment.

drawbacks.text: A flat 6% leverage ratio applies the same requirement to all institutions regardless of the riskiness of their assets, which supporters of risk-based capital rules argue is a blunt instrument that can penalize safe lending [S3].

The bill gives regulators broad escape valves: the Federal Reserve can adjust ratios, exclude foreign deposits from the liability caps, and grant emergency temporary exemptions, which could soften the limits in practice [S3].
Forcing the biggest banks to shed assets on a one-to-three-year clock could disrupt credit markets during the transition, a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real, costly problem: banks so large and so thinly capitalized that their collapse threatened everyone else, as 2008 showed. The size caps and 6% leverage floor directly reduce the chance of taxpayer-funded rescues and the bailouts that followed. The main counterargument is that blunt size and leverage rules are a crude substitute for risk-sensitive regulation and could push some lending into less-regulated channels, but the bill's off-balance-sheet disclosure rules address part of that concern.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee in April 2010, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio introduced the bill on April 21, 2010, joined by original cosponsors including Kaufman, Casey, Merkley, Whitehouse, and Harkin [S1][S3].
Seven senators in total cosponsored the bill: 6 of the Senate's 58 Democrats and 1 of 1 Independents [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, which took no further action recorded for the rest of the 111th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest bank holding companies and big nonbank financial firms, which avoided having to shrink, raise capital, or move assets off their books; smaller banks and depositors did not get the limits the bill offered.

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push for size caps and higher leverage requirements on the biggest banks.

against.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on the day it was introduced and never held a markup or brought it to a vote; it died there.

against.name: Large Wall Street banks
against.role: Biggest U.S. bank holding companies and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed caps on bank size and leverage during the 2010 financial-regulation debate, arguing they would hurt competitiveness and credit availability.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so there is no roll-call record; all 8 supporters were Democrats or the Independent, and the bill died in a Democratic-chaired committee without a vote.

industries.note: The 10% deposit cap and 2%-of-GDP liability cap would have forced the biggest banks to sell assets or break apart, and the 6% leverage floor would have required them to fund themselves with more of their own money instead of debt. The bill died, so they kept their size and their funding advantage.

Nonbank financial companies supervised by the Federal Reserve would have faced a 3%-of-GDP cap on nondeposit liabilities and the same 6% leverage floor. The bill never advanced, so no limits were imposed.

Caps on the largest institutions' deposit share and borrowing would have slowed the consolidation that pulls customers and market share toward national megabanks. They gained nothing because the bill died.

The SEC would have been required to force companies to record off-balance-sheet financings on their balance sheets, ending the practice of hiding liabilities from investors. The rule was never written because the bill failed.
